title: Escalate or Defuse
theme: Conflict and resolution: how disputes grow and end
objectives: I can describe how a conflict grows and how it can be calmed or settled.
I can tell mediate, arbitrate, and appease apart.
I can use words for the stages of a dispute in a short story, a discussion, and an argument.
I can use the endings -ate and -ation to move between a verb and its noun.
rationale: Conflict drives both history and fiction, and students need precise words for its whole arc. The ten words cover how a conflict builds (adversary, hostile, retaliate, escalate), when it stalls or cools (impasse, defuse, appease), and how it ends (mediate, arbitrate, reconcile). The unit also separates three often-confused ways of settling a dispute: mediate (help the sides agree), arbitrate (a neutral person decides), and appease (calm one side by giving in). Students already know bilateral and unilateral from the prefix unit and concession from the argument unit, so this unit lets them apply those words to a human dispute. Two endings, -ate and -ation, give practice in moving from a verb to its noun.

words.def: To help two sides settle a disagreement by talking with each and suggesting solutions.
words.ex: The counselor mediated between the two friends until they agreed on a plan.
words.ex2: A neutral neighbor can mediate a fence dispute better than either owner can.
words.nonExample: Taking one side and refusing to hear the other is not mediating.

apps.academic: A mediator listens to both sides and helps them find a solution they can accept.
apps.spoken: Can you mediate? We can't agree on the movie.
apps.writing: Use mediate when a third person helps the sides reach their own agreement.

words.def: To restore friendly relations after a quarrel, or to make two things agree.

words.ex2: It is hard to reconcile the bank's report with the numbers on the receipts.

words.def: To calm someone by giving in to what they want.
words.ex: The manager offered a refund to appease the angry customer.
words.ex2: Trying to appease the bully by giving him lunch money only made him ask for more.

apps.spoken: I only said yes to appease him.

passage.title: The Maple Tree on the Fence
paras: It began with a maple tree. Its branches hung over the fence between the Tran and Petrakis yards, shading Mrs. Petrakis's tomato garden and dropping leaves into Mr. Tran's gutters. At first the neighbors only grumbled, but a few small remarks quickly escalated. When Mr. Tran trimmed the branches without asking, Mrs. Petrakis retaliated by piling the cuttings on his driveway.

Within a month the two were adversaries. They stopped waving, their voices turned hostile, and even their children avoided each other at the bus stop. Mr. Tran tried to appease her by leaving a bag of peaches at her door, but she assumed that it was a trick and left it untouched on the step.

A volunteer from the community center, Ms. Rowe, offered to mediate. She seated them at a kitchen table and gave each of them ten minutes to speak without interruption. Slowly she defused the tension by asking questions that made each person describe what they really needed: shade for the tomatoes, clean gutters, and a little respect.

Still, the talks reached an impasse over who should pay to remove the lowest branches. Neither would move. Ms. Rowe suggested a different step. They could ask a retired forester, Mr. Idowu, to arbitrate, which meant that he would hear both sides and make a decision that both promised to accept.

Mr. Idowu studied the tree, listened to both neighbors, and ruled that they would share the cost of trimming twice a year. To everyone's surprise, the ruling brought relief rather than anger. A few weeks later the two reconciled over a basket of tomatoes and a plate of peach tart. “Next time,” Mrs. Petrakis said, “we will talk before we cut.”

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word “impasse” most nearly means
choices: a successful agreement
a long delay caused by bad weather
a road between two houses
a point where talks are stuck and neither side will move
qs.why: The sentence says neither would move, which describes talks that are stuck.

qs.q: Why does Mrs. Petrakis leave the bag of peaches untouched?
choices: She suspects the gift is a trick rather than a sincere attempt at peace.
She dislikes peaches.
She does not see the bag.
She plans to give them to Ms. Rowe.
qs.why: The passage says she assumed it was a trick, so she did not trust the gift.

qs.q: How is Ms. Rowe's role different from Mr. Idowu's role?
choices: Ms. Rowe cuts the tree, while Mr. Idowu waters the garden.
Ms. Rowe makes the final ruling, while Mr. Idowu helps them reach their own agreement.
Ms. Rowe helps the neighbors find their own agreement, while Mr. Idowu hears both sides and decides.
Both give orders without listening to either neighbor.
qs.why: Ms. Rowe mediates by asking questions, and Mr. Idowu arbitrates by hearing both sides and making a decision.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the dispute was escalating?
choices: The maple tree dropped leaves into the gutters.
Mr. Tran trimmed the branches without asking, and Mrs. Petrakis piled the cuttings on his driveway.
Ms. Rowe gave each neighbor ten minutes to speak.
Mr. Idowu studied the tree.
qs.why: Each action is a response that is bigger than the one before it, which is escalation.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Trees should be cut down before they cause trouble.
Neighbors who argue should avoid each other.
Experts always settle disputes better than neighbors can.
A dispute can grow when each side strikes back, but it can be settled when others help and both sides listen.
qs.why: The story moves from retaliation to mediation, arbitration, and reconciliation.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that describe the arc of a conflict: how it builds, where it stalls, and how it ends. They read a short narrative in which two neighbors escalate a dispute and then settle it, and they practice -ate and -ation word endings. A focus is separating three ways of settling a conflict: mediate, arbitrate, and appease.

notes.va.mediate.v: A mediator helps the sides reach their own agreement and does not decide. Role-play with a student mediator who may only ask questions. Contrast with arbitrate, where the neutral person decides.
notes.va.hostile.adj: Hostile is open unfriendliness or opposition, not simple shyness or dislike. Ask students to distinguish hostile body language from hostile words, and to suggest how to respond calmly.
notes.va.retaliate.v: Retaliate is a response to a hurt. Ask what the first harm was and whether retaliation made the problem smaller or larger. Avoid classroom use that treats a student's feelings as an offense.
notes.va.reconcile.v: Two uses appear: restoring friendship and making two accounts agree. Students will meet the second in math and social studies. Check that the sentence makes the intended sense clear.
notes.va.arbitrate.v: Arbitrate is a neutral decision that both sides accept in advance. Distinguish from judge in a trial, where a decision can be forced. Do not link it to arbitrary, whose everyday meaning is different.
notes.va.adversary.n: Adversary is a serious opponent, often in a contest. It does not need to mean hatred. Pair with ally as an opposite and ask students to name adversaries in a story they know.
notes.va.impasse.n: Impasse has a figurative meaning (a stalemate in talks), even though it began as a blocked road. Ask students what could break an impasse: a break, a mediator, a new offer.
notes.va.escalate.v: Escalate is a process in stages. Have students draw a staircase of a conflict, with one action per step, and then draw how someone could step down. The noun escalation is a good -ation example.
notes.va.defuse.v: The calming sense is figurative from the bomb sense, shown in senses. Ask what a person did, not just that the situation got better. Students may confuse defuse and diffuse; note the difference briefly.
notes.va.appease.v: Appease often has a slightly negative flavor: giving in to calm someone, sometimes at the cost of fairness. Contrast with mediate, which is fair to both. Ask when appeasing works and when it does not.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “When Mr. Tran trimmed the tree without asking and Mrs. Petrakis piled the cuttings on his driveway, she retaliated, and each step made the quarrel bigger, so it escalated. Ms. Rowe asked questions to help them agree, which is mediating. Mr. Idowu listened and decided, which is arbitrating. The difference is who makes the final choice.”
discuss: What is the smallest thing a person could do to defuse an argument?
When is it right to appease, and when does appeasing make things worse?
misconceptions: Mediate and arbitrate mean the same thing.
Appease always means to make peace in a fair way.
An impasse is a physical road.
Reconcile only means to become friends.
extend: Choose a conflict from a book or from history and map its stages with one unit word per stage.
Write a short dialogue in which a mediator helps two characters reach a concession.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to bilateral and unilateral: ask which kind of decision a mediator helps with and which kind an arbitrator makes. Revisit concession and contend as moves in a negotiation. Return to mediate, arbitrate, and appease two days later in a sorting task, again at one week with a news story, and in unit 10 when students examine a narrator's viewpoint on a conflict.
